problems.title: Whole-block commitment can violate target stopping semantics
problems.source_location: Sections 3.1 and 5.1; vispec/model/spec_model_ours.py, specgenerate; vispec/model/utils.py, update_inference_inputs
claim: The method relies on distribution-preserving speculative decoding, but the release appends a complete verified block before checking EOS and generation budget.
analysis: Choose unique greedy target outputs \(a\), then EOS \(e\), then \(b\) after that EOS prefix, and a matching draft path \((a,e,b)\). All positions satisfy argmax verification, but whole-block commitment returns \((a,e,b)\); ordinary stopped generation returns \((a,e)\). The GQA caller removes EOS strings without truncating the ordinary suffix. Independently, a budget \(M=2\) permits lengths \(2\) then \(3\) because the check is strictly greater after appending; a long block can overshoot even with a non-strict comparison. A separate Vicuna caller does truncate final text, limiting a repository-wide claim.
result: The released general routine does not guarantee the same stopped sequence under admissible EOS/cap boundaries. This does not measure the frequency or quality impact in pretrained benchmark outputs.
repair: Before commitment, truncate the verified block to the remaining budget and earliest stopping token. Advance counters and caches by the committed prefix length and stop immediately when exhausted. The prefix invariant proves stopping correctness conditional on valid target verification.
problems.impact_rationale: The local release violates stopped-output semantics at boundary cases, without establishing damage to the reported benchmark or core visual adaptor.
problems.existing_correction_status: The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: The baseline counter stays zero and speed accounting uses different units
problems.source_location: Section 5.1 and Table 1; gen_baseline_answer_gqa.py baseline generation; speed.py
claim: The baseline returns a generated-token field used for logging, while timing analysis is intended to compare cost per generated token.
analysis: The baseline initializes new_token to \(0\) and never updates it, despite appending tokens; the counter-based limit therefore stays inactive. A valid generated suffix \((7,8,2)\), with EOS \(2\), has length \(3\) but the returned count remains \(0\). Evaluation callers also omit a common explicit cap, leaving baseline/speculative defaults \(2048\) and \(512\). Contrary evidence matters: speed.py retokenizes cleaned baseline text instead of using the zero field, so zero recorded counts do not imply its denominator is zero. That script uses a fixed LLaVA tokenizer even for Qwen, while speculative counts use target token IDs; equality of those units is not guaranteed.
result: The release’s baseline field and budget plumbing are defective. Existing timing compensation prevents a direct zero-denominator allegation, and the effect on published speedups is unquantified.
repair: Set count from sequence length minus prompt length, pass the same explicit cap and stopping convention, and use comparable validated token units for both sides. Reanalysis requires the actual saved responses and timing records.
problems.impact_rationale: These are released measurement/provenance defects; no new benchmark or corrected speedup has been established.
problems.existing_correction_status: The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

impact_rationale: Minor: concrete stopping and accounting defects are present in current release paths, but the empirical speedup table and adaptor contribution are not independently disproved.
